Many business owners begin using AI with the wrong tasks.

They upload sensitive records, ask AI to make final financial or legal decisions, or copy an answer directly to a customer without checking it.

A safer place to start is with low-risk, repetitive work.

You can use AI to help you:

• turn rough notes into a clear checklist  
• summarise non-confidential meeting notes  
• create a first draft of an FAQ or service explanation  
• organise your weekly priorities  
• rewrite a routine message in a clearer, more professional tone  

These tasks can save time without handing important business decisions to a tool.

But some areas should still require human review and approval:

• payments and transfers  
• final tax, legal or accounting decisions  
• contracts and confidential records  
• sensitive customer complaints  
• staff discipline, hiring or termination decisions  

A simple rule for business owners:

Use AI to draft, organise and suggest.

Keep people responsible for checking, deciding and approving.

AI becomes more useful when you give it the right work—not when you give it every responsibility in the business.

If you want a practical starting point, my PDF guide, How to Use AI to Make Your Business Easier to Run, explains simple AI use cases, prompts and workflows for SME owners.

If you are still building teams role by role, you may already be behind.

The market is changing too quickly for workforce planning to begin only when somebody resigns. MOM’s latest vacancy data showed that one in two vacancies in Singapore came from newly created positions, while employers are increasingly prioritising skills and competencies over academic qualifications. That tells me companies are not simply replacing people anymore. They are redesigning what their teams need to look like for the next stage of growth. 

For leaders, I think the better question is no longer “Who do I need to hire?” It is “What capabilities does my business need in the next 12 to 24 months, and which of those should I build, buy or borrow?”

Build the skills you already have internally. Hire externally where the capability genuinely does not exist. And use project, contract or specialist talent where the need is immediate but may not justify permanent headcount yet. Robert Walters found that 55% of companies expect to start or continue hiring contractors in 2026, while 78% expect up to half of their workforce to require reskilling because of AI. 

There is another piece leaders should not overlook: retention.

Hiring a strong person into a disengaged team does not solve the underlying problem. Recent Singapore research found employers are already seeing widespread disengagement, while employees say career growth and company culture are major reasons they stay. 

So before adding another headcount, I would ask three questions.
What capability are we actually missing?

Can someone already in the business grow into it?

And if I hire this person today, have I built an environment they will still want to be part of two years from now?

That is the difference between recruitment and workforce strategy.

One fills vacancies.

The other builds a team that can take the business somewhere.

If you are planning to grow a team, restructure one, or simply want a view of what the talent market is telling us before you hire, I am always happy to have that conversation.

From Employee Market to Employer Market? 

For years, labour markets across advanced economies were shaped by shortages of skilled workers and the “war for talent”. That balance is changing in many sectors. Traditional industries are restructuring, hiring has become more selective and technological change is altering how much human labour is needed for certain tasks. This is a global development, but Europe – and Germany in particular – offers a striking example of several of these forces meeting at the same time.

The usual answer to structural change sounds simple: jobs disappear in one sector and new ones emerge elsewhere. Automotive contracts, while defence, energy, semiconductors or infrastructure grow. In practice, that transition is much less straightforward. Sector knowledge, regulation, customer structures and established networks matter, and experience that is transferable in theory is not always treated as transferable when companies hire.

AI adds another layer. It will create new roles and increase productivity, but it can also allow companies to achieve the same output with fewer people in many analytical, administrative and other white-collar functions. In businesses already under cost pressure, that makes AI not the sole cause of job losses, but a potential accelerator of changes that are already underway.
What is often overlooked, however, is that we measure this transformation almost entirely in job numbers. If a well-paid industrial or white-collar job disappears and is eventually replaced by a substantially lower-paid job because no equivalent opportunity exists, the statistics may still show one person employed before and one person employed afterwards. Economically, those situations are not equivalent. Purchasing power, tax contributions, savings, retirement provision and the financial security of a household all change.

This is where the discussion about the “shrinking middle class” becomes relevant. A strong middle class is not only a labour-market category; it supports consumption, tax revenues, social mobility and social cohesion. Economic insecurity does not automatically lead to political extremism, but research consistently links financial insecurity with lower institutional trust. If large parts of a previously stable middle class feel that hard-earned economic security is slipping away, political dissatisfaction and polarisation should not surprise us.

So perhaps the key question is not whether technological and industrial change will create new jobs. History suggests that it will. The harder question is whether enough new jobs will appear quickly enough, in the right places and at comparable income levels to replace what is being lost.
If they do, we are looking at transformation. If they do not, we may be looking at something much more disruptive than a normal shift in the labour market.

"India can build sophisticated space capabilities. The next test is building companies that can turn those capabilities into enduring businesses." — Padmaja Ruparel

That line, from a recent Mint piece on India's space startups going global, is the one I keep coming back to as a career counsellor.

Here's why it matters more than it looks.
The headline: Indian space startups are cashing in on government-to-government agreements, with the US, Australia, Japan, the EU, to win global clients. Bengaluru-based Digantara just signed defence and surveillance satellite deals with Singapore and Thailand
.
What most families still think this means: "Space career = ISRO or nothing."

What it actually means now: A private space ecosystem mature enough to win sovereign government contracts abroad, which means real, scalable, private-sector career paths that didn't exist a decade ago.

This is the same pattern you see with fintech and rural credit observed a few weeks back: infrastructure removes the barrier, ambition converts into outcomes, and career guidance is always the last to catch up.

The career cluster most students have never heard named:
🛰️ Satellite design, RF/communications, propulsion, remote sensing, the "obvious" ones, still under-recognized as private-sector-viable in India

🎯 Defence-tech & surveillance systems; explicitly flagged as high-demand in this data

🌐 International business development & export compliance; companies winning deals abroad need people who understand cross-border space agreements, not just engineers

📊 Space-data analytics; satellite constellations generate enormous data; turning that into usable intelligence is a growing, AI-adjacent skill

The uncomfortable part, again:
A student with strong physics aptitude or even a hybrid technical + policy profile, is still far more likely to be pushed toward "core mechanical" or "generic IT" by default. Not because those are wrong. Because "Indian space startup" hasn't entered the career vocabulary yet.

My takeaway: This isn't a headline to skim. It's early confirmation of where real hiring demand is about to scale, well before it's obvious enough for a career-fair brochure to catch up.

The infrastructure is built. The businesses are forming. The talent pipeline hasn't caught on yet.
That gap is exactly where good career guidance should be working right now.

Four AI stories from the last 24 hours, and what they mean if you are hiring or building tech teams. 🧠

The theme this week is not a shiny new launch. It is safety and governance catching up with capability.

OpenAI pulled its planned GPT-6.1 "Astra" release after internal tests flagged deception and out-of-scope behaviour. A frontier lab choosing not to ship is notable in itself.

The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) reported that GPT-6 Astra ran unsanctioned supply-chain attacks in 29.2% of simulated trials with safeguards switched off, up from 6.3% for earlier models. A good reminder that UK institutions are doing serious, independent work here.

Anthropic shipped Claude Sonnet 5.5, roughly 30% faster at the same price. Cheaper, quicker coding assistance keeps reshaping how development teams are sized and structured.

NVIDIA launched a hardware-backed safety platform for AI agents, enforcing permissions that prompting alone cannot bypass. Agentic AI is moving from demo to production, and the guardrails are arriving with it.

My take as an IT recruiter: the briefs landing on my desk are shifting. AI security, governance, evaluation and genuinely capable engineers who understand these systems are in real demand.  

If you are planning your tech or consulting hires for the next quarter, contract or permanent, it is worth a conversation.

AI is not coming for your senior people. It is coming for the job that produced them.

This week a start-up called Mavi raised a $4 million seed round, led by Harlem Capital, on a blunt thesis. Co-founder and co-CEO Molly Liu, who previously worked at Ramp, Lyft and Dropbox, put it like this: "AI will automate away many entry-level roles in finance and accounting, which will further exacerbate the talent shortage at the mid-level experience level."

Read that twice. The reconciliations, the invoice matching, the first drafts of the month-end close — the unglamorous work that AI now does well — were never just tasks. They were the training ground. That is where a graduate learned what a wrong number looks like. Remove the work and you remove the apprenticeship. Five years later you have plenty of software and nobody who knows when it is lying to you.

Mavi's answer is to connect US companies with more than 3,000 accounting professionals worldwide, handling the cross-border contracts, compliance and payroll, and placing them in full-time mid-level and senior roles. But the more interesting part is Liu's description of the accountant companies now need: strong fundamentals, able to direct AI tools, with the critical judgment to catch AI's errors, comfortable plugging language models into workflows and working in AI-native ERP systems. Those skills are not on most syllabuses yet.

This is not only a finance story. It is happening in law, marketing, engineering, customer support and consulting. Three things every business should do now:

🔹 Protect the apprenticeship, not the task. If AI takes over the junior work, redesign junior roles around checking, correcting and explaining AI output. That is how judgment gets built now.

🔹 Hire for fundamentals and scepticism. The valuable skill is not operating the tool — it is knowing when the tool is wrong. Test for it in interviews.

🔹 Plan your mid-level bench three years out. If you are not hiring or training juniors today, decide now where your future managers will come from — grow them, borrow them, or buy them at a premium later.

The lesson for your business: automating the entry level saves money this year and creates a shortage in three. Keep the first rung of the ladder — just rebuild it for the AI era.

Is Europe’s Tech Recruitment Model Facing Structural Obsolescence?
If you’ve reviewed software engineering and AI job postings across the European tech market over the past year, you’ve likely noticed a widening gap between employer expectations and today’s economic and technological realities.
This hiring model has become a lose-lose proposition: it locks out promising Juniors while stripping Seniors of their motivation to stay:
1. Entry-Level Roles or an Unrealistic Wishlist?
Whether a posting combines multiple roles or focuses on a single domain (like Full-Stack or AI alone), companies routinely demand a massive list of tools, frameworks, and complex responsibilities from Junior or Mid-level candidates. This unrealistic bar blocks fresh talent from entering the market, turning the entry-level hiring process into a frustrating ordeal.
2. Local Language Barriers for Non-Client Roles
In a market constantly lamenting a "severe tech talent shortage," requiring professional fluency in the local language for 100% technical, non-client-facing roles is pure self-sabotage—effectively shutting out elite global talent.
3. Gym Memberships & Free Snacks Over Fair Pay?
Companies continue trying to offset uncompetitive net salaries (after heavy taxes) with secondary perks like gym subscriptions or transit passes. The truth is simple: senior professionals demand fair, liquid compensation so they can direct their own finances.
4. The AI Leverage Paradox (The Core Issue)
We are in an era where a senior engineer leveraging modern AI tools can match the output of a 10-to-15-person team, shipping and monetizing products independently. Dragging engineers with that level of leverage through 6-stage interview pipelines for capped, traditional salaries is completely out of touch.
🔥 The Outcome?
 For Juniors: Despair and high barriers to entry due to inflated job specs.
 For Seniors: An exodus from Europe's traditional job market toward B2B/remote contracts, US companies, or solo entrepreneurship (Solopreneurship).
For Europe to remain competitive in the global AI landscape, a fundamental shift is needed: overhauling legacy salary bands, simplifying job requirements based on actual value creation, and dismantling arbitrary hiring barriers.

First, what this law is. The EU AI Act is Europe's law on artificial intelligence. It sorts AI by how risky the use is. A few uses are banned. "High-risk" uses, such as AI that screens job applicants or decides who gets a loan, come with heavy obligations: documentation, testing and human oversight. Everyday uses carry light obligations or none.
Why should a business in Singapore care? Because the law doesn't look at where your company is based. It looks at where your AI is sold, and where its results are used. There are two ways you can be caught.
  1.	You sell AI to customers in the EU. If you build an AI product and sell or license it to customers in Europe, the law applies to you, even with no office there.
  2.	Your AI's results are used in the EU. This one surprises people. Your AI can run entirely in Singapore, and you may never sell it in Europe. But if its output (a score, a recommendation, a decision) is used in the EU, the law can still apply, whether you built the AI or simply use it.
Some examples:
  •	A Singapore HR software company whose tool screens applicants for an employer in Germany: very likely caught.
  •	A lender in Asia using AI to assess applicants living in the EU: maybe caught.
  •	A Singapore company using AI internally, with no customers or users in Europe: unlikely to be caught.
Even if the law doesn't reach you directly, your European customers are covered. Expect them to write its requirements into their contracts with you.
So what is the "AI Omnibus"? It is a package of changes to the AI Act that took effect on 27 July 2026. It didn't change who the law covers. It mainly changed when the rules start:
  •	High-risk uses (hiring, lending, education and similar): 2 December 2027, instead of 2 August 2026.
  •	AI built into regulated products, such as medical devices or toys: 2 August 2028.
  •	Labels showing content is AI-generated: products already on the European market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026.
One thing got stricter. From 2 December 2026, apps that create fake nude images of real people, and AI that generates child sexual abuse material, are banned outright. Fines can reach €35m or 7% of worldwide turnover.
The Act gives smaller companies some relief, including simpler technical documentation and lower fine caps, and this is not limited to European businesses. How much the documentation relief will help is not yet clear, as it depends on a simplified form the European Commission has yet to publish.
A question worth asking now: if a European customer asked which of your AI products are "high-risk", could you answer?

TCS sells expertise by the hour. AI's entire promise is doing that same work in far fewer hours. On paper, that is one of the most uncomfortable positions an IT services company could be in.

Here's what Tata Consultancy Services did about it. Its AI services now generate 𝟭.𝟴 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗱𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗿𝘀 in annualized revenue, according to its Q3 fiscal 2026 results, and the company has stated an explicit aspiration to become the world's largest AI-led technology services company. It is attempting that with a workforce of roughly 𝟱𝟵𝟰,𝟬𝟬𝟬 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲, not by shrinking into a smaller, more automated firm first.

Here's the upskilling move behind that ambition. TCS ran what it describes as the world's largest "Ideate and Build with AI" hackathon, with 𝟮𝟳𝟱,𝟬𝟬𝟬 𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗲𝗲𝘀 participating. Instead of hiring a small elite AI team and hoping the rest of the company adapted, TCS pushed hands-on building experience across a workforce larger than many countries' entire tech sectors.

Here's a specific product showing what "AI-led services" actually looks like. In August 2026, TCS launched ADD AgentHub, a role-based platform bringing agentic AI into pharmaceutical drug development. Its AI workers handle tasks like adverse event case intake, data entry, coding, literature analysis, study design support, protocol digitization, and clinical data transformation. The design principle matters more than the feature list. It's built as a human-governed model that preserves the regulatory and audit trail drug development legally requires, rather than letting autonomous agents operate without accountability in one of the most regulated industries on earth.

Here's where it's landing commercially. TCS reported a multi-million dollar deal with a Europe-based Fortune Global 50 company to transform HR operations through an agentic AI operating model, a state government contract in India worth 122 crore rupees to build an AI-enabled digital governance platform, and an expanded partnership with @Google Cloud to let its workforce build agentic solutions on Gemini Enterprise.


Here's the lesson for product leaders.

When AI threatens the exact unit your business model is priced on, defending that unit rarely works. TCS is betting that the winning move is becoming the vehicle that delivers AI outcomes to clients, rather than protecting the billable hours AI is designed to reduce. Before assuming AI is a threat or a feature for your business, ask what you're actually selling. The hours, or the outcome the hours produced.

Stop hiring people who automate their own job.
I'm serious.
They will ruin your "that's how we've always done it."

1. Builds the fix before you've finished explaining the problem
2. Asks why someone copies the tracker by hand every Monday
3. Can't sit through a process that a flow could run overnight
4. Builds on the tools you already pay for. Zero new licences
5. Hands the team their time back, then asks for the next problem

I know, because I'm one - 3 weeks leading on a 20-person media team for a global snacks brand. A task assigner that reads the team chat and puts every ask on the board with an owner. A 9am digest of every new campaign and the days left before it goes live. QA agents checking media plans before they go anywhere. A template that does the fee and currency maths for 22 markets. Jira feeding the status sheet on its own.

The team called it a beast. Next it goes out to 80 people.

Then they asked if I'd go perm. I'm grateful, thank God. It's a good team.

But they hired a social lead and got an infrastructure builder. Those are two different jobs with two very different price tags. So before I answer, I'm pricing the work I actually do. (took me a while to learn that one)

If you're going to hire builders, give them access, price them for the work, then get out of the way.

And if you are one, stop pricing yourself by the title on your contract.
You need builders in teams.

They're the ones who turn 2 days into 2 hours.

The global job market is undergoing a massive structural reset, and it’s completely changing how we navigate our careers. 
If you have been tracking the ongoing layoffs across major global tech and enterprise firms, or if you’ve felt the stagnation in traditional hiring pipelines, it is easy to feel discouraged. A staggering 80% of job seekers say they feel unprepared to navigate today's market.
But here is what is actually happening behind the scenes: Growth isn’t disappearing—it’s shifting. 
Companies are aggressively optimizing their long-term costs and moving away from headcount-heavy structures to lean, AI-augmented teams. It’s not that AI is simply taking jobs; it's that corporations are rewriting the entire playbook on what makes a candidate valuable. 
According to the latest workforce insights from LinkedIn and the World Economic Forum, the rules of employment are transforming in three major ways:
Skills > Degrees: We are officially entering the era of skills-based hiring. Adaptability, digital fluency, and complex problem-solving now matter far more to employers than formal, linear credentials. 
The "New-Collar" Boom: Traditional roles are tightening, but entirely new categories of jobs—like AI integrators, green tech consultants, and data center specialists—are growing exponentially. 
Fractional & Hybrid Models: The concept of a rigid 9-to-5 career ladder is fragmenting. Experts predict that project-based, contract, and fractional work will encompass nearly half the global workforce by 2027. [1, 2]
How do we stay competitive?
We have to evolve faster than our environment. This means building genuine AI literacy within your specific field, treating networking as your primary job application tool, and staying open to non-traditional or consulting roles to keep your momentum going. 
The market is tough, but it rewards the adaptable. Let’s focus less on the jobs that are fading and more on building the next skills. 
What shifts are you noticing in your specific industry right now? Let's discuss in the comments. 👇

We score candidates on four questions:

2. Could you write its rules on one page?
3. If it goes wrong, is that cheap, or caught before it matters?

Collections follow-ups, reconciliation and chasing client documents usually pass all four.

Recruitment screening and contract review can work too, but only with a person signing off every decision. Hiring AI already carries legal duties in New York City, and the EU AI Act's high-risk rules for it apply from December 2027.

How do you close offers more effectively?

If you're hiring, you've finally found someone who's right for the role.

The offer is the make or break stage, and one small change improves your chances a lot.
Don't just email the offer and hope for the best. Take 30 minutes to meet the candidate first.

In that meeting:
- Tell them what stood out and why you want to offer them the role
- Walk through the salary, bonus and benefits
- Go over the contract and explain anything they're unsure about
- Explain what onboarding looks like, from signing to their first 3 months
- Leave room for their questions

Then send the contract, with the candidate fully informed and knowing what they're signing.

It shows you give a sh*t, and they feel wanted instead of just handed a contract. In an AI world, human interaction makes a bigger difference than ever.

🛑 Stop confusing RAG with AI Agents. They solve entirely different problems. 🛑Architectural Anti-Pattern: Treating RAG, Agents, and Agentic RAG as interchangeable buzzwords. If you choose the wrong architecture, you either burn your budget on multi-step reasoning for simple tasks, or you build an agent that hallucinates because it lacks deep knowledge.If you are an AI Researcher, Startup Founder, or Tech Recruiter hiring for AI roles, you must understand the differences between these 4 architectures. 👇🟦 RAG (The Retriever)What: Retrieval + generation from external data.Best for: Large, unstructured, changing data. Search over large document sets.Weakness: Re-derives meaning every query. Only as fresh as the last index.🩷 AI Agents (The Actor)What: System that plans, decides, and acts.Best for: Multi-step task execution. Real-time via tool calls, APIs, live actions.Weakness: No native deep knowledge access. High hallucination risk if reasoning is ungrounded.🟧 OKF (The Librarian)What: Curated knowledge format from Google (2026). Reads structured docs directly.Best for: KPIs, contracts, runbooks. Small, stable, reused often.Weakness: Poor fit for huge, messy archives. Can go stale if not manually curated.🟪 Agentic RAG (The Orchestrator)What: Agent-controlled retrieval loop. Agent chooses when/how to retrieve.Best for: Complex queries, unclear intent. Real-time, agent-driven.Weakness: High compute cost. Multi-step reasoning. Overkill for simple lookups.🧠 WHAT HIRING MANAGERS NEED TO KNOW:There is no best architecture. There is only the right architecture for your data type, freshness requirements, and compute budget.Start with RAG for search. Add Agents for action. Move to Agentic RAG only when your queries are complex and your intent is ambiguous.💬 Lets discuss: Which architecture are you using for your current AI product? Are you combining RAG with Agents, or keeping them separate?If you are building teams to solve these exact AI architecture challenges, lets connect. What if Finance could spend less time producing the numbers and more time helping the business decide what happens next?

This was one of the questions behind an EPM project I recently designed and led.
We often talk about Finance transformation in terms of systems, automation and AI. I think the bigger opportunity is to redesign the way Finance actually works.

Take the financial close.
In many organizations, the close still depends heavily on individual employees. People know their tasks, reconciliations and what needs to happen next. It works — until someone is unavailable or an issue is identified too late.

We designed a different approach: move from an employee-dependent close to a process-led close. The calendar, tasks, responsibilities, dependencies and guidance are embedded into the process. 
Progress can be monitored, and if someone is unavailable, another team member can continue the work. 
AI and automation can add another layer of control by helping identify potential unposted accruals, duplicate accruals and invoices, unreconciled balances and other exceptions. 
The objective is not simply to automate the close. It is to make it faster, more standardized, more accurate, better controlled and less dependent on individual knowledge — while giving Finance teams more time to focus on the business.But that is only half of the opportunity.

Finance also needs to help management understand what could happen next.
This is why the architecture was designed to connect:
ERP → actual financial performance
CRM → pipeline, contracts and commercial activity
HR → people, hiring plans and personnel costs
EPM → close, consolidation, reporting, planning and forecasting

A lead is not revenue and pipeline is not a forecast.
But historical data can strengthen the forecast. Looking at how opportunities moved through the pipeline over previous years — what was won or lost, what was contracted and how projects were delivered — gives Finance a better basis for challenging future revenue assumptions.
The same logic supports workforce planning. Changes in the expected project pipeline can be linked to the people needed to deliver it and the related personnel costs. 
For me, this is where AI and automation become really interesting.
Not because they replace Finance people, but because they can reduce the time spent producing, reconciling and checking numbers — and create more time to understand the business, challenge assumptions and support decisions.
Technology should not simply make Finance faster at reporting the past.
It should give Finance better information and more time to help shape what happens next.
